questions.prompt: Why does a JSONL log survive a crash better than one JSON array rewritten after every event?
options: JSONL files are compressed, so writes finish sooner
A crash can only damage the unfinished last line; earlier lines are never touched
JSON.parse reads JSONL files faster than arrays
JSONL files are written by the operating system, not your program
questions.explanation: Appending only adds bytes at the end, so finished lines stay intact. Rewriting a whole array means a crash mid-write can leave a file that is not valid JSON at all.

questions.prompt: minidsh calls fsync once per batch instead of once per event. What does it trade off?
options: It risks corrupting earlier lines in exchange for speed
It skips writing some events to save disk space
It saves time, but a crash can lose the whole unfinished batch rather than one event
It makes the file unreadable until the batch is complete
questions.explanation: fsync is slow, so one per batch is cheaper. Events in a batch whose fsync never finished were never confirmed as saved, so losing them breaks no promise.

questions.prompt: loadEvents finds bytes after the last newline. Why does it truncate the file instead of only ignoring them?
options: So the next appended line is not glued onto the broken bytes
To reclaim the disk space those bytes use
Because the header line must be the last line in the file
Because fsync fails on files with a torn tail
questions.explanation: The next append adds bytes at the end. If the torn bytes stayed, the new event would be joined to them on one line, and that line would never parse.
